title: “We’re Afraid on a Daily Basis”: How a Maryland Sheriff Targeted Immigrants Long Before ICE Raids Spiked
author: Alex Burness
content:
**The brothers crammed their lives into backpacks.** The younger one cried
when he hugged his cats goodbye. “They were everything to me,” he says.

They were headed from San Salvador to a new life in Frederick County,
Maryland, some 2,000 miles away, where their family had contacts and where
their mom, fleeing for her life, had already relocated, along with their
stepfather.

The journey would be dangerous, but not as dangerous as staying. Growing up in
El Salvador’s capital, both brothers had witnessed gang murders by the time
they were 11 years old, and both feared that they themselves could be killed
if they turned down the wrong street. The family business, a hair salon, had
been extorted to the point that it no longer made money.

They crossed rivers and highways, traveling by foot for long stretches. They
survived crooked police and robbery along the way, first in El Salvador and
Guatemala and then more often in Mexico. They slept on hard floors and their
young bodies ached.

When they finally arrived in Frederick, they were quickly plugged into a local
network of support, as this was, and still is, a fast-growing area with lots
of Latino immigrants and many thousands of non-citizens, their mother and
stepdad included. It’s been almost a decade since they got here, but they
still recall an early bit of guidance: “We heard from our community that the
sheriff’s office is racist,” the older brother says. “We have heard people
saying that many times.” (_Bolts_ is not publishing the names of the brothers
and other immigrants interviewed for this story because they’re vulnerable to
arrest.)

The longtime sheriff in Frederick County, Chuck Jenkins, [earned this
reputation](https://boltsmag.org/sheriff-chuck-jenkins-and-immigration-
frederick-county-maryland/) by associating with far-right, anti-immigrant
organizations designated as hate groups by the Southern Poverty Law Center.
Jenkins, a Republican who stands for re-election this November, has become a
small-town celebrity who has been a Fox News regular and visited with Donald
Trump at both the White House and Mar-a-Lago.

He was an early supporter of Trump, who he said in a 2015 interview is “right
on the mark” on immigration.

“As long as I am sheriff of Frederick County, we are going to work with ICE,”
[Jenkins said](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MWAz9_leOVY) in that interview,
“and we are going to take the criminal aliens—as many as we can—out of
Frederick County.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_8425-2400x1800.jpg)Frederick County Sheriff Chuck
Jenkins was first elected in 2006 on an explicitly anti-immigrant platform.
(Photo by Alex Burness)

Jenkins matched his rhetoric with policies that targeted immigrants in his
community. While hundreds of sheriffs around the country, [including many in
Maryland](https://boltsmag.org/maryland-287g-contracts-with-ice-growing/),
have lately rushed to partner with ICE to assist in arresting, jailing, and
ultimately deporting immigrants, Jenkins was doing this long before it was
fashionable: In 2008, two years after he took office, Jenkins became one of
the first sheriffs in the country to join ICE’s 287(g) program, which
deputized his staff to question people’s immigration status inside the local
jail. In the 18 years since signing that contract, Jenkins says, his office
has used 287(g) to send about 2,000 people into ICE custody for deportation.

“The fear and the justified state of terror and hysteria that folks have been
put in nationally under this administration is what folks have been living
under in Frederick for years,” Frederick resident Sebastian Brown, an advocacy
strategist with the ACLU of Maryland, told me. “People didn’t always know the
name 287(g), but they knew that if you got sent to jail, you’d end up with
ICE. That fear has been here since 2008 and permeated every part of people’s
lives.”

Among Jenkins’ claimed 2,000 ICE referrals was the Salvadoran brothers’
stepdad. One morning last summer, two weeks after their mother gave birth to a
baby boy, the stepdad left for work and never came back. A sheriff’s car had
followed him, and then he was apprehended by a deputy while picking up work
supplies from a local store. He had no criminal record and wasn’t sure why
he’d been stopped, but was hauled to the county jail nevertheless.

The older brother says a jail staffer was rudely dismissive when he called
that day to find out what had happened, and that he was told the matter had
“nothing to do with” him. When the stepdad was able to call home, he relayed
that jail staff had told him he’d be released after 48 hours.

“We went there right after the 48th hour to wait for him outside,” the older
brother says. “We waited for three hours, and nothing. We tried to call him. …
No answer, no information.”

The brothers would later learn that their stepfather never came close to
release, because ICE took custody of him at the jail, transferred him to the
agency’s own jail in Baltimore, then flew him to yet another jail in Texas,
where he spent two miserable months and lost a lot of weight, before finally
being deported last fall.

Bills added up for the family left behind, since the stepdad has supported
them all financially. The younger brother dropped out of college. Their mother
eventually self-deported, taking their baby brother, plus another younger
sibling, back to El Salvador. The brothers who stayed in Frederick now
struggle to afford food and seldom leave home.

“In our community, the Hispanic community, there is always a fear of being
stopped by the sheriff office,” the older brother says.

“We are afraid on a daily basis,” he continues. “We like to go hiking a lot.
And there is always this thought in the back of our minds, like, what if ICE
is there, in the forest? It’s horrible because there are things you really
enjoy, but the joy just vanishes when you think of that.”

Their mother had built a hair salon inside their new home, picking up the
career she’d left behind in San Salvador. She’s gone now, but the salon
remains untouched. The brothers try not to go in there because it reminds them
of her. Their stepdad’s drill and circular saw are collecting dust on the
kitchen floor. In the garage, a baby car seat is growing moldy.

* * *

**Jenkins is well known for his crusade against immigrants in his community,**
making [declarations](https://www.aclu-
md.org/app/uploads/drupal/sites/default/files/1_-_medrano_v_jenkins_compl.pdf)
like “the single biggest threat to our country is the immigration problem,”
and, “We cannot continue to absorb this population or we will end up in
collapse like a third world country.” After he first took office in 2006, Fox
News named him the second-toughest sheriff on immigration in the whole
country—behind only Joe Arpaio, the former Arizona sheriff notorious for his
racial profiling of Latinos.

Jenkins’ platform became [part of a larger
backlash](https://boltsmag.org/sheriff-chuck-jenkins-and-immigration-
frederick-county-maryland/) against the rising immigrant and Latino population
in Frederick County. As Jenkins started working hand-in-glove with ICE to
arrest and deport immigrants, local officials declared English to be the
official language in the county, attempted to restrict landlords from renting
to undocumented people, and even tried to make public schools report their
undocumented students to authorities.

Local immigrant rights advocates say that Jenkins’ rhetoric and close
collaboration with ICE has undermined public safety by discouraging immigrants
from calling police when they witness or are victims of crime. In Frederick
County this month, I met with many immigrants who have had family, friends,
and neighbors deported, which they say has made them more afraid of local
police, especially the sheriff’s office.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_8684-copy-2400x2068.jpeg)The hair salon inside the
brothers' Frederick County home sits vacant since their mother self-deported
along with their baby brother. (Photo by Alex Burness)  

One immigrant woman told me she didn’t call 911 after she was recently
involved in a car crash, even though she needed help. The younger of the
Salvadoran brothers, who saw his family ripped apart by the deportation of his
stepfather last year, told me, “My friends don’t feel safe to call the police,
because they think that’s going to get them deported. They don’t feel
freedom.”

While the Trump era helped embolden Jenkins’ attacks on the immigrant
community in Frederick County, the ground has also started to shift beneath
him in recent years. The county has become much more liberal as it’s grown in
population; George W. Bush carried it by 20 percentage points in 2004, but by
2024 the county population had grown by 50 percent, and Kamala Harris won it
by nine points.  

Karl Bickel, a top official in the sheriff’s office during the 1990s and the
Democratic nominee for sheriff in each of the last three cycles, lost by 26
points when he first ran against Jenkins in 2014. But he’s gotten much closer
with each run, losing by 4 points in 2018 and just 2.8 points in 2022.

I met Bickel, who is again challenging Jenkins this November, at a coffee shop
in outer Frederick County on a recent Sunday morning. As he has for the past
12 years, Bickel continues to promise voters to take the sheriff’s office in a
much different direction, saying he would shun collaboration with ICE and use
the office as a check on a federal agency that he says has acted lawlessly.  

“The sheriff’s office, once informed ICE is doing anything in the county,
would respond,” he said about his plans for the office. “A deputy, or two
deputies, and a supervisor would respond, to monitor the activity. We’d find
out who the ICE supervisor is, ask them if they have a warrant, and find out
what their mission is. They might cooperate and they might not.” He says he’d
direct deputies to record these interactions with ICE and produce reports on
the agency’s local activities that he would post publicly online.

“A lot of what ICE is doing, if a deputy did it they’d be fired or arrested,”
he told me. “The use of force, the utilization of chemical agents, things like
that. It’s just not right.”

Much has changed since Bickel’s last unsuccessful run for sheriff. For one,
Democrats in the Maryland legislature, responding to Trump’s mass-deportation
scheme, passed legislation early this year [banning local 287(g)
agreements](https://boltsmag.org/maryland-new-mexico-ban-local-contracts-with-
ice/). In a [companion
bill](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Legislation/Details/SB0791?ys=2026RS),
Democrats also significantly restricted other, more informal ICE
collaboration, blocking police in the state from questioning people’s
immigration status in most cases, and blocking most forms of information
sharing between local agencies and ICE.

These changes, among other effects, forced the cancellation of Jenkins’
contract with ICE, and that of the eight other Republican sheriffs in Maryland
who’d signed up for the program. Jenkins, who strongly opposed the changes,
joined 16 other Maryland sheriffs this summer in suing the state to block some
of them.

All of the sheriffs who joined the
[lawsuit](https://marylandmatters.org/2026/05/27/county-sheriffs-file-lawsuit-
challenging-community-trust-act/), which repeatedly refers to immigrants as
“criminal aliens,” are running unopposed in November—[non-competitive sheriff
elections are typical](https://boltsmag.org/sheriff-elections-virginia-2025/)
in this country, even in swing counties—save for Jenkins and Republican
Jeffrey Gahler of Harford County.

Bickel says that, if elected, the other sheriffs in the state “wouldn’t like
me.” And the differences between him and Jenkins could hardly be more stark,
both in policy and personality.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_8361-2400x1800.jpg)Karl Bickel has challenged
Frederick County's GOP sheriff Chuck Jenkins for each of the past four
election cycles. (Photo by Alex Burness)

Bickel, who is 76, hasn’t been active in law enforcement in decades; when we
took a drive to the county jail together, he wasn’t sure where to park at
first because, he said, he had not been there in at least 10 years. He says he
doesn’t enjoy campaigning and portrays himself as a bookish intellectual; when
we met for coffee, he literally toted four books to demonstrate his reading
prowess, and, wearing an American University hat and his class ring, noted
several times that he’s received much more formal education than Jenkins. “Ask
him what the last book he read was,” Bickel remarked. “My guess is there won’t
be one.”

At a farm across town, I met Jenkins as he gathered with some 200 supporters
for a barbecue. Jenkins, who rarely misses a local parade or festival, is a
natural in this setting. A radio host and a Republican lawmaker lauded him
from a microphone, praising the sheriff for having survived a “witch hunt”—a
nod to the [federal indictment](https://www.justice.gov/usao-md/pr/frederick-
county-sheriff-and-gun-dealer-indicted-scheme-illegally-acquire-machineguns)
against Jenkins in 2023 on charges of conspiring with a local gun store owner
to illegally acquire machine guns, which prosecutors later
[dropped](https://marylandmatters.org/2024/11/12/federal-prosecutors-to-drop-
charges-against-frederick-county-sheriff/) during the final days of the Biden
administration. Multiple senior Jenkins staffers approached me to say that
they’ll quit their jobs if the sheriff loses in November.

When Jenkins and I stepped away from the cookout to talk, the sheriff blasted
the recent legislation that killed his ICE contract and forced him to change
his jail policies. In the past, the jail had what he called “our 287(g)
investigative room,” where deputies would “investigate where that person was
from, how they got here.”

“If they were in the country illegally, we’d have access to all the ICE
databases,” Jenkins said, “and based on that we’d prepare a detainer for ICE.”

According to Jenkins, the state has effectively shut down coordination between
his office and ICE. Now jailers just ask about what country a detainee was
born in and where they have citizenship. “But we don’t screen for immigration
status anymore,” Jenkins lamented.

While Jenkins criticized the policy changes, he saved most of his venom for
Bickel, calling his perennial challenger a “treacherous prick.” Jenkins, who
is 70, worked under Bickel’s command at the sheriff’s office during the 90s
and considers him “devious.”

“I’m going to tell you what, man to man: I’d kick his ass, personally,”
Jenkins told me. “Physically. I’d stomp his ass. Someday, he’s got an ass-
kicking coming. I don’t like the son of a bitch. Personally, politically, he’s
no good. He can read all the books he wants.”

* * *

**Amid the fear of law enforcement that Jenkins’ rhetoric and policies have
heightened for immigrants in Frederick County,** many in the community have
organized to protect themselves to the extent possible. They’ve alerted one
another in encrypted group chats about ICE activity, watched each other’s
children, and delivered groceries to people who are scared to leave home.

The recent state reforms, and the restrictions they’ve put on Jenkins’
operations, are still cold comfort for immigrants in Frederick County as ICE
enforcement has exploded across the state and country. “Immigrants know there
wasn’t a change of heart, but a change of law,” says Maryland immigration
attorney Viviana Westbrook, who has worked with many Frederick County
residents. “All these years of this kind of messaging is not going to be wiped
away by one bill, or by several bills.”

Much of the organizing and mutual aid in Frederick County are conducted by
people who are themselves vulnerable to deportation, like the woman recently
involved in the car crash, who told me that when she began coordinating
grocery delivery in May, she and colleagues had a list of 15 families who
needed help.

“Now, it’s more than 50,” she tells me as we sit together in her living room.
“In four months it’s grown that big. And these are only the families we know
of.”

She tells me about one mother she’s helping, whose husband was arrested last
month. “Now she has no idea how she’ll take care of the kids. The father was
the earner of that household. She can’t pay for her apartment. It’s very
difficult.”

She adds, as her daughter plays on the couch, “I’ve witnessed the harm this
does to the children, psychologically. To not see your mom or your dad is
impossible. How can we help that situation? You continue because there’s no
other way, but a child—what can they do?”  
  
The woman says she knows parents who have withheld their kids from school this
year and says she knows others who do send their kids to school but who
decline to enroll them in free-lunch programs out of fear of even the
friendliest of government interactions. State data show [a drop in Latino
enrollment](https://www.fredericknewspost.com/news/education/schools/maryland-
hispanic-student-enrollment-declines-amid-immigration-
fears/article_1796f22b-b810-51e5-aac9-4b8d6af8de88.html) across Maryland
schools, and in Frederick County specifically, as the immigration dragnet
forces vulnerable families into hiding.

After a little while, a friend of the woman swings by. She’s a mother to young
children, and among the dozens of immigrants receiving food aid in Frederick
County. She tells me about her husband, who was arrested last year and
deported: “He worked in roofing. We had a normal life,” she says.

Her husband, who she says had no criminal record, was stopped by ICE on the
way to work, for no clear reason. “People said they were only taking
criminals, people with records. But when they took him we realized it’s not
that way,” she says. This sort of apprehension is now common for ICE; 70
percent of people in its custody have no criminal record, according to
Syracuse University’s [immigration
database](https://tracreports.org/immigration/quickfacts/).

The wife of the deported man continues: “When you’re with your partner you
know how to deal with things. It’s not always easy, but you know. When you’re
alone it’s much more difficult.” One of her children is in therapy and
sometimes comes home from school crying. “I try to be strong, so they don’t
see me down,” she says.

This family’s story is familiar in Frederick County, where immigrants and
attorneys for many years have alleged a pattern of racial profiling in traffic
stops. In 2019, the ACLU of Maryland [sued](https://www.aclu-
md.org/app/uploads/drupal/sites/default/files/1_-_medrano_v_jenkins_compl.pdf)
Jenkins’ office on behalf of an immigrant woman who’d been pulled over by a
deputy for a purported taillight issue, and then interrogated about her
immigration status.

After being detained on the roadside for nearly an hour while the deputy tried
to get an ICE agent to respond, the woman, Sara Medrano, was released with a
warning for a nonfunctioning taillight, which she says was working just fine
when she checked it later that night.

The lawsuit accused Jenkins of pursuing a policing strategy that “treats
immigrants as second class” by subjecting them to “unlawful and
unconstitutional interrogation, seizure and detention” based on race and
ethnicity. A 2021 [settlement](https://www.aclu-md.org/press-releases/victory-
lawsuit-over-frederick-county-sheriffs-racial-profiling-latinx-people/) in the
case awarded $25,000 in damages to Medrano and forced Jenkins to issue her a
written apology for what she’d endured. As part of the settlement, the
sheriff’s office also agreed to implement training to try and prevent racial
profiling and to conduct public meetings about its role in immigration
enforcement, including its participation in the 287(g) program.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_9199.jpg)Frederick
residents protested against ICE agents who came to the city for enforcement
operations in early September. (Photo courtesy of
[@missmouse.bsky.social](https://@missmouse.bsky.social))

For the first few years, when ICE was seldom spotted in this area, those post-
settlement public meetings were lightly attended. The most recent one,
however, was standing room only. Residents one by one aired complaints about
the posture of the sheriff’s office toward immigrants.

Notably, however, attendees say that none of the speakers that day were actual
immigrants directly vulnerable to ICE. “That tells me they’re afraid,”
Westbrook said.

Following the state reforms passed this year, officials like Jenkins are
technically prohibited by law from questioning people they stop based on
suspected immigration status. But even so, last year the U.S. Supreme Court’s
conservative majority [ruled](https://www.scotusblog.com/2025/09/justice-
brett-kavanaugh-and-racial-proxies/) that federal immigration agents could
racially profile people for apprehensions, and advocates and immigrants in
Frederick County say this happens often.

“People are getting picked up every day. Early morning, after work, at
worksites, getting pulled over,” says Brown, of the ACLU of Maryland. “With so
much increased funding, ICE has replaced the role, with welcoming, open arms
from the sheriff’s office.”

He adds, “287(g) was a force multiplier for ICE, but now they’re sending
people to Frederick and cutting out the middleman.”

* * *

**This new dynamic was on display in early September,** as ICE descended on a
quiet Frederick neighborhood for a multi-day stakeout. Many residents
responded in protest, helping to escort children home from school, sharing
information in private channels, waving anti-ICE signs, and even linking arms
in the street to try to prevent ICE movement. ICE agents [reacted
violently](https://marylandmatters.org/2026/09/08/officials-demand-answers-
after-violent-ice-confrontation-with-frederick-protesters/); an agent beat at
least one protester with a baton, according to video obtained by _Maryland
Matters_.

The stake-out would have been an unusual sight two years ago. But ICE’s
increased presence locally has galvanized citizen activists—including many who
otherwise did not previously participate in such resistance.

ICE opponents across the county say that if Jenkins were to finally lose this
November, it would be a credit to the growing outrage of voters who might not
have heard of 287(g) before, or who might not have considered Jenkins’ agenda
closely in the past. That shouldn’t be an insurmountable challenge; after all,
Jenkins has won only narrowly in each of his last two contests with Bickel.
And the city of Frederick, which is the county seat, seems to have only gotten
more liberal since, as evidenced in part by local immigrant rights leader
César Díaz not only winning a seat on Frederick’s city council last fall, but
then immediately ascending to become the council president.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_8705-2400x1800.jpg)Local immigrant rights leader
César Díaz joined the Frederick City Council last fall. (Photo by Alex
Burness)

The first ordinance the new council passed was called the [City Values
Act](https://cityoffrederick.granicus.com/MetaViewer.php?view_id=12&event_id=5989&meta_id=196754),
which prohibits city employees from assisting ICE without a judicial warrant
and bans ICE from using city property for any enforcement activities. That
followed another reform, passed in 2024, [allowing non-citizens to
vote](https://www.wmar2news.com/local/non-citizens-living-in-the-city-of-
frederick-will-soon-be-allowed-to-vote) in certain local elections. (Even so,
[almost none actually have voted](https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/9-non-
citizens-voted-fredericks-045900487.html), fearing interaction with any level
of government.)

But the city is a very different place from the outlying county, which is
mostly quite rural and much more conservative, and which has helped carry
Jenkins to victory after victory even as Frederick County’s electorate has
gotten bluer.

Díaz said he believes Jenkins can be defeated this year because more local
voters now seem to care about immigrant protection, which has helped raise
awareness of the sheriff’s record.

“The worse things get with the Trump administration, the more support the
immigrant community gets,” Díaz told me. “I don’t go two days without someone
new reaching out to see how they can help. Every week I’m talking to 10 people
or more who are asking, ‘What can we do?’ It’s becoming less and less distant
for people. Every day, more people know someone who knows someone, or they
know someone directly, or it’s their kid’s friend at school, or their
neighbor, or their co-worker.”

The damage to the community, Díaz says, has become impossible to ignore.
“Every week we have seven, eight, 10 different families being affected by ICE.
Dads who leave for work and don’t come back.”
